Charles de Hémard de Denonville (1493–1540) was a French Roman Catholic bishop and cardinal who played a crucial role in the religious and political landscape of Western Europe during the late 15th and early 16th centuries. As a key figure in the Catholic Church, he was instrumental in shaping the religious doctrine and policies of the time. Denonville's significance extends beyond his individual achievements, as he was part of a larger network of religious and political leaders who shaped the course of European history. His legacy continues to be felt in the modern Catholic Church, and his actions had far-reaching consequences for the Protestant Reformation and the Counter-Reformation. Despite the passage of time, Denonville's impact on the religious and political history of Western Europe remains a testament to his enduring influence.

Born in France around 1493, Denonville rose through the ranks of the Catholic Church to become a cardinal, serving as a bishop in the Diocese of Paris. His tenure as bishop was marked by controversy, as he clashed with rival factions within the Church and engaged in power struggles with secular leaders. Denonville's most notable achievement was his role in the Council of Trent, a major ecumenical council that sought to reform the Catholic Church and address the theological and disciplinary issues that had arisen during the Protestant Reformation. The council's decrees had a profound impact on the development of Catholic doctrine and practice, and Denonville's involvement in the council helped to shape the Church's response to the Reformation.

entities.summary:
Charles de Hémard de Denonville (1493–1540) was a French Roman Catholic bishop and cardinal who played a pivotal role in the early days of the Protestant Reformation.

Born into a prominent aristocratic family, Denonville served as a diplomat for the Holy See before being appointed as Bishop of Auxerre in 1514. His tenure was marked by controversy, particularly his involvement in the affair of Joan of Arc's canonization, which led to his exile from France in 1520.

Denonville later returned to France and became a key figure in the Council of Trent, where he contributed to the development of the Catholic Church's response to Protestantism. His efforts helped shape the Counter-Reformation movement, which would have far-reaching consequences for European religious politics.

Despite his significant influence on the course of Christianity, Denonville's legacy has largely been overshadowed by other figures of his era, making him a fascinating case study for historians seeking to understand the complexities of 16th-century religious conflict.

The sheer scale of the Protestant Reformation – with millions of adherents and countless institutions established across Europe – speaks to Denonville's enduring importance in shaping Western history.
